title: The AI Hype within Investing... a Step Too Far- - Systematic Investor 301

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/The AI Hype within Investing... a Step Too Far- - Systematic Investor 301.docx

summary: Systematic Investor 301: Rob Carver and Niels Kaastrup-Larsen on trend following vs tail hedging, VIX carry across the roll, why a systematic trader makes no election adjustments, and why LLMs in trading invite overfitting. Also fees and vol-adjusted fee comparison.

coverage.note: Nvidia commoditized chips; trend allocation timing and weak mean reversion
portfolio P&L, positioning and risk at half target
trend barometer, CTA index numbers, put-buying listener question
options trading experience; theory of negatively correlated hedge
overpriced downside vol; leveraged vs unleveraged tail hedging
tail hedge cost; trend vs puts; leverage danger
tail protection vs trend use cases; crisis alpha; roll carry question
VIX curve carry and election kink; back-adjusted series
roll carry immaterial; UK election politics
political risk through equity risk premium; US election
no system adjustments; three steps of political trading
market reaction difficulty, Brexit; AI hype intro
AI hype skepticism and LLM limits
overfitting result, AI liability, fees intro
allocators and incentive fees; costs known returns unknown
nothing actionable: wrap-up and sponsor read

completeness_estimate: 0.72 - the first reader caught the main arguments (tail hedging, trend vs puts, VIX carry at roll, elections, LLM overfitting, fees) but missed supporting data (index returns, positioning), the fee hurdle and two-tier points, UK fiscal comments and several caveats from Niels.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: There is a sort of weak mean reversion effects in trend-following returns.
claims.claim: Trend-following returns show weak mean reversion, so adding allocation after a modest drawdown is better timing than adding at a high watermark.
claims.direction: add trend allocation after a modest drawdown
claims.conditions: weak effect only; market timing is hard
claims.testable: partly - test allocation timing on trend index returns

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the thing about chips is is is one of those businesses that that has gradually got more commoditized over time.
claims.claim: Chip businesses (memory, CPUs, smartphone chips) have become commoditized with thin margins, so Nvidia's position is unusual and its highly rated stock reflects unpredictable shifts in leadership.

correction.issue: Mixes two speakers and overstates the margin point: Carver said memory chips are microscopic-margin, while CPU margins are 'better' but still commoditized; the remark on unpredictability of who would be talked about (Nvidia 2-3 years ago) is Niels's, not Carver's.
correction.fix: Carver: memory chips are heavily commoditized with microscopic margins, CPUs and smartphone chips are less so but also commoditized; Nvidia is the surprise. Niels adds that Nvidia's rise shows how unpredictable leadership is.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Um my risk is running at just under 10% annualized standard deviations. That's about just under half of my kind of long-term target.
claims.claim: After trends reversed or weakened, a volatility-targeted trend system automatically runs at about half its long-term risk target because forecasts and positions shrink.
claims.conditions: after drawdown with weak trends
claims.testable: yes - compare realized risk to target

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: my biggest short position actually is VIX. So, that's very much a pro risk-on um position
claims.claim: A short VIX position is effectively risk-on (long equities) because VIX falls when investors think equities are getting less risky, so the book is net long equity beta.
claims.direction: short VIX with long equity indices
claims.conditions: when equity trends are up
claims.testable: yes - correlation of positions with equities

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the markets that have done well have been uh interest in the effects, particularly yen
claims.claim: Mid-2024 P&L: FX (yen, euro, Swiss franc), Asian equities (Taiwan, Nikkei) and cocoa were profitable while energies (gas) and metals (gold, platinum) lost money.
claims.indicator: sector P&L of a trend portfolio
claims.direction: long FX and Asian equities; losses in energy and metals

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: My own trend barometer is super weak. So in line with performance numbers it's 25
claims.claim: A trend barometer at 25 is close to the weakest level normally seen, in line with trend-follower performance in June 2024 (BTOP50 -2.79%, SG CTA -3%, Trend Index -3.57%) while equities rose.
claims.conditions: after strong Q1, difficult Q2 for trend followers; fixed income and metals challenging

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a portfolio with a 2% allocation to insurance and a 98% allocation to S&P 500 can theoretically achieve a higher geometric return
claims.claim: Spitznagel's claim: a 2% allocation to far out-of-the-money puts and 98% to the S&P can beat the S&P on geometric return despite a negative expected return on the puts.
claims.indicator: systematic deep OTM put buying plus monetization
claims.conditions: requires a monetization rule when a crash occurs

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: buying optionality is is in the long run a long losing strategy because we because of the variance premium because of the insurance premium if you like.
claims.claim: Buying options is a long-run losing strategy because of the variance (insurance) premium, while selling volatility is dangerous in different ways around events.
claims.direction: short volatility earns premium; long optionality loses

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's actually possible to improve the expected um either sharp ratio geometric return both can be improved by adding an asset to your portfolio that has a negative return but is negatively cause a negatively correlated
claims.claim: Adding a negative-return asset that is negatively correlated with the portfolio raises the Sharpe ratio, which allows more leverage and hence a higher geometric return.
claims.conditions: hedge must be strongly negatively correlated

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there was once a 25% down day in the S&P 500 in 1987. There has never been a 25% up day.
claims.claim: Equities are negatively skewed in the tails (1987 -25% day, no +25% day), so strategies with negative skew justify tail protection when leveraged.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: people overprice volatility, but they overprice downside volatility even more
claims.claim: Out-of-the-money downside puts are systematically overpriced because investors hedge crashes, not rallies, and bid-offer spreads on far-OTM options are wide, so put buying persistently loses money.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I'm a bit skeptical as to why you need to buy tail protection, to be honest, because you're you're only going to see the costs and not the benefits
claims.claim: Unleveraged long-horizon investors (e.g. endowments) face no margin-call risk, so tail protection only reduces their return; it makes sense only for leveraged investors.
claims.conditions: investor has long horizon and no leverage
claims.testable: partly - compare returns with and without hedge

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: any tail-risk manager that tells you they're going to give you their insurance policy for free, I'd be a bit skeptical.
claims.claim: A tail-risk fund that buys puts only selectively (when cheap) may leave the investor unprotected at the moment of need, so claims of free insurance are suspect.
claims.testable: partly - fund track records in crisis

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if it's going to cost you 2% of your portfolio to defend yourself against a you know, a 50% drawdown, that seems to me to me quite reasonable
claims.claim: Paying about 2% per year for tail protection can be reasonable for a leveraged book because protection allows higher leverage; at 30% cost it does not.
claims.direction: modest tail hedge for leveraged portfolios
claims.conditions: hedge cost small relative to leverage gain

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: option strategies as kind of first responders in a crisis and then trend following was like the second responder
claims.claim: Option strategies respond to a sudden crisis first while trend following helps in prolonged drawdowns but may not help in the initial phase.
claims.indicator: options vs trend following crisis response
claims.conditions: trend works in prolonged bear markets, random in fast crashes
claims.testable: yes - compare strategy returns in crisis phases

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: If you add um trend following to a uh long only portfolio, you can improve your geometric return
claims.claim: Adding 10-30% trend following to a long-only portfolio raises Sharpe and geometric return without extra leverage because it has positive expected return and low correlation to markets.
claims.indicator: trend following allocation share in a traditional portfolio
claims.conditions: uncorrelated; no extra leverage

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you add a big slug of trend following say 30%. Um it's quite plausible that your your risk is going to fall
claims.claim: Adding trend following to a levered risk-parity portfolio lowers measured risk, tempting investors to lever up; in a crisis where trend also loses, all assets fall together with large leverage.
claims.conditions: when trend does the wrong thing in a crisis

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's dangerous to describe trend following as a crisis alpha strategy because no crisis is the same
claims.claim: Trend following should be seen as a non-correlated return strategy rather than crisis alpha because each crisis differs and trend response is not guaranteed.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the spot VIX is about 13.4.
claims.claim: VIX futures curve in contango (spot 13.4, then 15, 16.5, just under 19 in October) predicts roll-down, which is the carry signal behind a short-VIX position and reflects the gap between expected and realised vol.
claims.conditions: curve upward sloping

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: November expiry and actually the December expiry as well, they're actually lower than October.
claims.claim: VIX futures for November and December price below October because of the US election on 5 November, so event risk shows up as a kink in the term structure that changes carry signals when rolling.
claims.indicator: VIX futures curve around US election
claims.conditions: around event dates

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I think it's more common to do what I do, which is form a single back adjusted price series of continuous contract
claims.claim: Computing trend and momentum on a single back-adjusted continuous price series avoids a forecast change at roll, whereas per-contract calculation changes positions at roll for no real reason.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Do I really care? Um, implementing what Lewis suggested would make my system a lot more complex
claims.claim: Using carry of the held contract at roll versus a smoothed continuous series is an immaterial approximation; the EMA smoothing of carry absorbs the change, though seasonal markets like crude and gas are more affected.
claims.conditions: stronger seasonality in crude and natural gas

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there are essentially um two things that that that kind of can affect markets in terms of political risk. One is the effect it has on, you know, what we would call the the equity risk premium
claims.claim: Political risk affects markets through the equity risk premium (drastic change raises required returns), and equity is a call option on enterprise value so volatility can even help.
claims.conditions: if change is drastic

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: this thing's on a knife edge, it could go either way.
claims.claim: The 2024 US election was finely balanced, and markets (VIX in October) priced a Trump win as the riskier outcome.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: and the correct answer is nil. Nothing. Nothing.
claims.claim: A systematic trader should make no system adjustment for elections, referendums or payrolls, because trading political macro requires predicting the outcome, its implications and the market reaction better than everyone else.
claims.testable: partly - compare rule-based vs discretionary overrides

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's no good predicting a foregone conclusion. No one's going to give you any any kind of P&L for that.
claims.claim: Political event trading needs three steps (outcome, implications, market reaction), and the last is hardest because reactions are unpredictable (Brexit moved euro-dollar unexpectedly) and consensus outcomes are already priced.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if we look at the the share prices of of not of Nvidia, but if you look at other companies that have done a very strong pivot to AI, um they're not doing so well
claims.claim: Companies that pivoted to AI (other than Nvidia) have not done well, suggesting AI hype is not translating into returns.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: this assignment, which for what it's worth, involves analyzing some some returns data from a strategy and comparing it to a couple of benchmarks, is is kind of AI-proof.
claims.claim: General large language models give meaningless platitudes on real data analysis tasks, so they are poor tools for evaluating strategy returns.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's very unlikely that that you'll you'll get that kind of rigor using the LLM.
claims.claim: Using off-the-shelf LLMs to find predictive patterns in financial data carries high overfitting risk and gives no statistical uncertainty or in-sample/out-of-sample discipline, unlike transparent fitting.
claims.conditions: user does not understand the technology

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Renaissance Technologies. The I mean, you know, nobody knows what they do, but it's probably that cuz they aren't doing what
claims.claim: Non-linear patterns in financial data may exist that classical statistics miss (Renaissance hires AI specialists), but that is very different from applying generic LLM tools.
claims.conditions: requires deep expertise

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Get up to 10, and you're you've got
claims.claim: In an experiment fitting up/down sequence patterns, as pattern length rises from 1 to 10 periods (up to 1,024 patterns) in-sample returns improve until the equity curve is a straight line while out-of-sample performance deteriorates; simple one-lag trend following stays similar in and out of sample.
claims.conditions: number of patterns grows exponentially

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: what about the liability? What about the liability of a firm using AI in its models
claims.claim: AI used in trading models without supervision and transparency raises liability and explainability issues, unlike transparent trend rules where the output is known.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I always say that costs are known and returns are unknown.
claims.claim: Since costs are known and returns are not, between two new managers choose the cheaper one, while established managers with great net returns (Renaissance) keep high fees.
claims.conditions: absent other information on performance

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you should always look at fees adjusting for volatility
claims.claim: Compare fees after adjusting for volatility target: 2-and-20 on a 25% vol CTA equals 1-and-10 on half the vol, so CTAs look cheap relative to low-vol long/short funds.
claims.conditions: comparing high-vol CTAs with low-vol equity funds

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: in in late April, I actually reached a high watermark of about um which would have So, the year-to-date figure would have been 16%
claims.claim: Carver's own trend allocation went from +16% year-to-date at the late-April high to about +7.8% by late June right after he added allocation at the high, in line with trend indices: an anecdote of buying a trend fund at its high watermark.
claims.conditions: Single anecdote, in line with CTA indices.
claims.testable: partly - fits the weak mean-reversion claim only anecdotally

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: market timing is very difficult, as we as we always say, which is why we leave it to to our models to do that.
claims.claim: Even a systematic trader who made an allocation timing mistake concludes that timing is too hard to do by judgement and should be left to the model.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I'm long MIB, which is the Italian stock index.
claims.claim: Carver's mid-2024 positioning: long equity indices (MIB, AEX, Nikkei, Nasdaq, S&P), yen and euro, cattle, short bonds and short VIX; cocoa was closed by the trend reversal. This is a positive-beta, pro-equity book with the roll (carry) position pointing the same way.
claims.direction: long equities, FX, cattle; short bonds, VIX
claims.conditions: Derived from trend and carry signals at the time.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think fixed income has probably been one of the more challenging sectors so far as far as I can tell.
claims.claim: After a very strong Q1, trend followers had a difficult spring: fixed income was whipsawed by inflation data and hopes of rate cuts (Europe cutting, the Fed holding out), and metals were hard; Europe's equities lagged the US after the European elections.
claims.indicator: fixed income trend P&L; inflation data; Fed path
claims.testable: partly - sector P&L by month is observable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Beta 50 down 2.79 for the month of June, up 6.41 uh, for the year.
claims.claim: In June 2024 the CTA and trend indices were down 2 to 4% (SG CTA about -3%, Trend Index -3.57%, Short Term Traders -1.93%) while year-to-date they were +0.8% to +7.7% against MSCI +11.6% and S&P 500 +15.5%, so trend followers lagged a strong equity rally.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG CTA, Trend Index, Short Term Traders Index, MSCI, S&P 500 YTD
claims.direction: trend lags equities in a narrow rally

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it would appear to be dependent upon a systematic program of buying far out of the money put options because you don't know in advance when the fast equity crash will occur, and then a monetization strategy
claims.claim: The Spitznagel result requires two pieces: a permanent systematic programme of far out-of-the-money puts (the crash date is unknowable) and an explicit rule to monetise the puts when volatility spikes (listener question relayed by Niels).
claims.conditions: Without the monetisation rule the payoff is not captured.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: geometric return is is all the the kind of ultimate I write about it a lot but it's the ultimate performance measure it's what everything comes back to essentially.
claims.claim: Geometric (compound) return is the right ultimate performance measure, which is why a Sharpe-improving but return-reducing asset can still help once leverage is allowed.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: typical negatively skewed trading strategy. And then that could be something like FX carry, an extreme emerging market FX carry, but it could also just be buying stocks
claims.claim: Negatively skewed strategies include FX carry (especially emerging-market carry) and long stock holdings, particularly individual stocks, which are prone to sudden sharp losses.
claims.direction: carry and long-equity returns have sharp left tails

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the drawdown being so fast that I can't de-risk my portfolio, and I'll basically lose all my money.
claims.claim: For a leveraged book the danger is a gap drawdown too fast to de-risk, which vol-targeting cannot prevent and only an option or similar hard floor does; this is the case for tail protection.
claims.conditions: Needs high leverage, e.g. 4x S&P.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if you're paying 2% every year for 10 years, you know, it becomes meaningful.
claims.claim: A 50% drawdown happens less than once per decade, so paying 2% a year for protection accumulates to a large drag over ten years and the benefit must be compared with that.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Leveraged investors should buy tail protection but should be wary of buying trend following if they're going to then use that as an excuse to apply even more leverage.
claims.claim: Match the tool to the investor: leveraged investors should buy tail protection (guaranteed payoff in a crash), unleveraged investors should buy trend following (positive expected return); trend must not be used to justify extra leverage.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the fact that that often governments spending more than they earn can be a good thing for example.
claims.claim: Carver believes UK policy dialogue ignores that government deficit spending can be beneficial, and that a more counter-cyclical (he says pro-cyclical) fiscal stance since 2010 would have left the UK better off.
claims.conditions: Opinion, no evidence given.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: nearly caused the entire UK financial system to disintegrate overnight, which is quite impressive.
claims.claim: Liz Truss's badly communicated economic plan nearly broke the UK financial system overnight, which is why both UK parties compete to look fiscally prudent: fiscal credibility shocks hit markets hard.
claims.direction: gilt yields up, sterling down on fiscal credibility loss

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: generally think that the Labour Party and the Conservative There's not going to be that much difference as far as the markets are concerned, at least initially.
claims.claim: A foregone election with near-identical platforms (UK 2024) creates little market uncertainty, unlike a close election with very different candidates.
claims.conditions: Holds when policy convergence is credible.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the US has a sort of system where you can lose the popular vote or do very badly in the popular vote and still become president
claims.claim: In the US system the popular vote does not decide the winner (2016), so even a lead in national polls leaves the presidency near 50/50.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I think everyone believes that that that, you know, if if the the crazy guy does get in, he's going to do crazy things.
claims.claim: In 2016 markets assumed Trump would be moderated by technocrats; by 2024 nobody believes it, so a Trump win is priced as a higher policy-risk outcome and the October VIX is bid up.
claims.conditions: Rob's reading of consensus, not a measured quantity.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's all very well to be interested in this and read the news, but it doesn't mean I should actually do anything
claims.claim: Staying engaged with political news is a behavioural trap: the more it plays on the mind, the harder it is to resist overriding the system, so the rule is to hold the position of 'do nothing'.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I think if you if you are you do think you can predict political outcomes, then, um, there are websites certainly in the UK where you can bet directly on the political outcome.
claims.claim: If you believe you can forecast an election, express that on a betting site rather than by overriding the trading system, keeping the view separate from the systematic book.
claims.conditions: Legality varies by country.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: actually, for the record, a lot of policies have been maintained actually under Biden, so, uh, you know, you never know what you get, uh, with these elections
claims.claim: Niels's caveat to Rob: many Trump-era policies were kept under Biden, so campaign rhetoric overstates the policy change an election produces.
claims.testable: partly - continuity of policy can be measured

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: They talked about how it reached $120 trillion in 2023.
claims.claim: A BCG report puts global asset-management assets at $120 trillion in 2023 yet the industry faces fee compression, rising costs and passive competition.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I am starting to see a bit of kind of, um, you know, skepticism creeping to my Twitter feed about AI
claims.claim: Carver reads rising AI scepticism on social media, alongside weak share prices of non-Nvidia AI pivots, as a sign that the hype is fading.
claims.conditions: Anecdotal sentiment reading.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: a lot of the people you're allocating to are still charging quite, you know, hefty incentive fees and incentive fees that don't have a hurdle, right?
claims.claim: Many managers charge incentive fees without a hurdle, i.e. on total return including cash interest instead of only excess over the risk-free rate, which matters most when rates are high.
claims.indicator: incentive fee hurdle vs risk-free rate
claims.conditions: Material when short rates are high (50bp vs 500bp).

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you guys are talking a big game, but actually when you look at who you're investing in
claims.claim: Ted Seides's point: allocators say they push hard on fees but keep investing in high-fee managers, so there is no real negotiation; investors really care about net performance (Renaissance), not the fee level.
claims.testable: partly - allocator behaviour can be studied

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: we were kind of going to end up with is a two-tier system where anyone, um, who's starting a who's starting a fund in the last few years is is going to have much lower fees
claims.claim: Fee structure becomes two-tier: new funds charge less, established funds with track records keep high fees, and raising fees later is awkward for seed investors.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I'm not in that camp. I don't believe that uh, to be uh, the right thing to do for our industry
claims.claim: Niels disagrees with competing on the lowest fees: CTA fees have already fallen over 35 years to reasonable levels, strategies cost money to run, and net returns are what matter.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: fees on some of the legacy funds we had were just you know, eye-popping
claims.claim: Legacy fund fees were very high because they were launched in the early 1990s when interest rates were higher and trail fees to advisers were part of the model; the fee margin has come down since.
